items.question: What does the AW139 RFM require each time an operating limitation is exceeded?
options: Make an entry in the log book describing which limit was exceeded, for how long, the extreme value and any relevant details.
Only inform maintenance verbally at the next inspection.
Reduce power to within limits and continue flight with no further action.
Note the exceedance mentally and write it down only if a defect occurs.
items.explanation: Section 2 GENERAL states that every limitation exceedance must be recorded in the log book with limit, duration, extreme value and other information needed for maintenance.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – GENERAL (p.2-1)

items.question: A torque limit is briefly exceeded during flight. According to the AW139 Normal Procedures, the crew should:
options: Ignore it if all indications return to normal.
Record the event in the log book with limit exceeded, duration, extreme value and relevant details.
Only inform ATC and continue normally.
Reduce airspeed and note the exceedance after landing only if vibrations are present.
items.explanation: The RFM requires a formal log book entry for any operating limitation exceedance, not just if secondary symptoms occur.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – GENERAL (p.2-1)

items.question: In AW139 Section 2, checks marked with the large special symbol are required:
options: Before each take-off.
Only before the first flight of the day.
Only after maintenance.
Only during IFR operations.
items.explanation: The note in GENERAL states that checks marked with the special symbol are required only before the first flight of the day; all others are for each flight.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – GENERAL (p.2-1)

items.question: According to AW139 FLIGHT PLANNING, what is the recommended order when using CAT B data and H–V charts?
options: Determine the H–V avoid area first, then CAT B weight.
Determine CAT B take-off and landing weight from the W.A.T. chart, then confirm the applicable H–V avoid area.
Use only the H–V diagram; CAT B charts are not used in planning.
Use Section 4 performance charts first, then Section 1 limitations, then H–V only if icing is present.
items.explanation: The text describes first determining CAT B weight from the W.A.T. chart, then confirming the H–V avoid area for those conditions.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – FLIGHT PLANNING / CAT B WEIGHT AND H–V DETERMINATION (p.2-1–2-3)

items.question: Which statement best describes how the CAT B W.A.T. and H–V charts are used together in AW139 flight planning?
options: The W.A.T. chart gives maximum weight and the H–V chart shows if any avoid area exists at that weight and altitude.
Both charts are used only for Category A operations.
The H–V chart determines maximum weight and the W.A.T. chart only confirms temperature limits.
They are used only when operating from grass surfaces.
items.explanation: Examples in Section 2 show using the CAT B W.A.T. chart to find allowable weight and then the H–V chart to determine whether an avoid area exists.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – CAT B WEIGHT AND H–V DETERMINATION (p.2-2–2-3)

items.question: In the GROSS WEIGHT AND CENTER OF GRAVITY section, which of the following is part of the recommended procedure?
options: Consult Section 6 for weight and balance data and ensure computed take-off and landing weights and CG lie within Section 1 limits.
Use only fuel quantity indications as long as CG is within envelope.
Assume CG is acceptable if weight is below maximum gross weight.
Skip landing weight calculations when operating under VFR.
items.explanation: The procedure explicitly calls for using Section 6 and Section 4 to compute take-off and landing weight and confirming weight and CG limits from Section 1 are not exceeded.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – GROSS WEIGHT AND CENTER OF GRAVITY (p.2-4A)

items.question: For cold weather operation in the AW139, what is required if the helicopter is parked outside at or below a specified OAT?
options: At or below -10 °C, fuel must be drained from all tanks.
At or below -20 °C, both main and auxiliary batteries must be removed and stored in a heated room.
At or below 0 °C, landing gear doors must be locked open.
At or below -15 °C, rotor blades must be removed.
items.explanation: Section 2 states that if the helicopter is parked outside at or below -20 °C, both Main and Auxiliary batteries should be removed and stored in a heated room.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – COLD WEATHER OPERATION (p.2-4A)

items.question: After cold soaking at or below -20 °C with batteries removed, what must be confirmed before flight according to the AW139 RFM?
options: That only the main battery is installed.
That both main and auxiliary batteries have been installed before flight.
That the batteries remain in the heated room until after take-off.
That battery voltage is below 23 V.
items.explanation: The text states that both Main and Auxiliary batteries should be removed and later confirmed installed before flight.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – COLD WEATHER OPERATION (p.2-4A)

items.question: When must the DAILY FUEL DRAIN CHECK be carried out according to the AW139 Normal Procedures?
options: At the end of the last flight of the day.
Before the first flight of the day, before moving the aircraft, by a trained person.
Only when water contamination is suspected.
Only during scheduled maintenance.
items.explanation: Section 2 requires a fuel tank drain check before the first flight of the day, before moving the aircraft, and specifies it must be done by a trained person.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – DAILY FUEL DRAIN CHECK (p.2-4B)

items.question: How much fuel should be drained from each fuel sump water drain valve during the AW139 daily fuel drain check?
options: 2–5 cc from each sump.
10–20 cc from each sump.
50–100 cc from each sump.
Until no more water is visible, regardless of quantity.
items.explanation: The procedure calls for draining 10 to 20 cc from each fuel sump water drain valve.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – DAILY FUEL DRAIN CHECK (p.2-4B)

items.question: After draining fuel during the DAILY FUEL DRAIN CHECK, what must be confirmed?
options: That fuel contains at least some water so the drains are working.
That fuel is free of water and no fuel is dripping from the aircraft drains.
That fuel colour has turned darker.
That drain valves remain open to ventilate the system.
items.explanation: The RFM states that after draining 10–20 cc from each sump, fuel must be free of water and there must be no fuel dripping from the drains.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – DAILY FUEL DRAIN CHECK (p.2-4B)

items.question: In the DAILY FUEL DRAIN CHECK description, the term 'trained person' refers to:
options: Any crew member on board.
Only maintenance engineers.
A mechanic or pilot who has received sufficient training to perform the task.
Only the aircraft commander.
items.explanation: The text defines a trained person as a mechanic or pilot who has received sufficient training to perform the fuel drain check.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – DAILY FUEL DRAIN CHECK (p.2-4B)

items.question: In the AW139 Pilot’s Pre Flight Check, what area is designated AREA N°1?
options: Fuselage – right-hand side.
Helicopter nose.
Tail boom – left-hand side.
Cabin and cockpit interior.
items.explanation: Figure 2-1 and associated text identify AREA N°1 as the helicopter nose.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – Pilot’s Pre Flight Check (p.2-5)

items.question: During the AW139 pre-flight walk-around in AREA N°1 (helicopter nose), what is one of the specified checks?
options: Verify main rotor blades are locked.
Check nose exterior condition, tie-downs removed, pitot-static probes uncovered and unobstructed.
Remove tail rotor tie-downs.
Confirm baggage compartment nets are installed.
items.explanation: AREA N°1 items include nose exterior condition, removal of rotor tie-downs and unobstructed pitot-static probes.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – Pilot’s Pre Flight Check (p.2-5–2-6)

items.question: What is checked on the nose landing gear during the AW139 external pre-flight?
options: Only tyre pressure.
Condition, shock strut extension, leaks and tyre pressure.
Only that the gear doors are open.
Only brake disc temperature.
items.explanation: The checklist item for the nose gear specifies condition, shock strut extension, leaks and tyre pressure.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – Pilot’s Pre Flight Check (AREA N°1, p.2-6)

items.question: For the ventilation air intakes in the landing gear bay during pre-flight, what does the AW139 checklist require?
options: Confirm they are closed to prevent FOD.
Ensure they are unobstructed.
Check that ice is present for anti-icing test.
Verify they are painted red.
items.explanation: The item reads 'Ventilation air intakes (in landing gear bay) — Un-obstructed.', so they must be free of obstruction.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – Pilot’s Pre Flight Check (AREA N°1, p.2-6)

items.question: In the baggage compartment checks on the AW139 walk-around, what must be confirmed?
options: Only that the baggage door is closed.
Condition of the compartment, cargo correctly secured with nets if installed, and baggage door secure.
That the compartment is empty.
That the baggage door is open for ventilation.
items.explanation: AREA N°2 and later areas specify checking compartment condition, cargo correctly secured by nets and that the baggage door is secure.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – Pilot’s Pre Flight Check (p.2-7–2-9)

items.question: In the cockpit/cabin interior (AREA N°7), which item is part of the AW139 pre-flight check?
options: Cabin interior equipment and cargo secure, first aid kit and cabin fire extinguisher on board.
All seats folded to maximise cargo space.
Cabin lights OFF at all times.
Passenger doors open and unlatched for quick boarding.
items.explanation: The checklist calls for checking cabin equipment and cargo secure, first aid kit present and cabin fire extinguisher secure and charged.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – Pilot’s Pre Flight Check (p.2-9)

items.question: In the AW139 COCKPIT/ENGINE PRE-START SAFETY CHECKS, what should be done with the ELT switch on the instrument panel?
options: Set to OFF.
Set to ARM.
Set to TEST.
Set to ON for continuous transmission.
items.explanation: The checklist item states 'ELT switch on instrument panel — Confirm ARM.'
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – COCKPIT/ENGINE PRE-START CHECKS (p.2-11)

items.question: During AW139 pre-start cockpit checks, what is the required position of the landing gear lever?
options: UP.
NEUTRAL.
DOWN.
Any position is acceptable on the ground.
items.explanation: The COCKPIT/ENGINE PRE-START CHECKS specify 'LDG GEAR lever — Confirm DOWN.'
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – COCKPIT/ENGINE PRE-START CHECKS (p.2-11)

items.question: What does the AW139 pre-start checklist require regarding circuit breakers?
options: All circuit breakers pulled for safety.
Only avionics circuit breakers engaged.
All circuit breakers engaged.
Only hydraulic circuit breakers engaged.
items.explanation: The COCKPIT/ENGINE PRE-START CHECKS include 'Circuit breakers — All engaged.'
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – COCKPIT/ENGINE PRE-START CHECKS (p.2-11)

items.question: According to the AW139 pre-start checks, what is the correct initial position of ENG 1 and ENG 2 MODE switches?
options: FLIGHT.
IDLE.
OFF.
Any position if ECL is at FLIGHT.
items.explanation: Item 6 in the safety checks specifies 'ENG 1 and ENG 2 MODE switches — OFF.' before start.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – COCKPIT/ENGINE PRE-START CHECKS (p.2-11)

items.question: How should the AFCS (autopilot) be configured during the AW139 COCKPIT/ENGINE PRE-START checks?
options: AFCS fully engaged in all modes.
AFCS engaged in heading mode only.
AFCS not engaged.
AFCS in ALT HOLD.
items.explanation: The checklist includes 'AFCS — Confirm not engaged.' before start.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – COCKPIT/ENGINE PRE-START CHECKS (p.2-13)

items.question: When carrying out the full and free flight control check with the electric hydraulic pump, what caution does the AW139 RFM emphasise?
options: Move all controls rapidly together to stress-test the system.
Move controls slowly and one at a time to avoid overloading the electric pump.
Use manual pumping only; electric pump use is prohibited.
Keep collective fully up during the check.
items.explanation: A CAUTION states that full and free checks should be carried out with slow displacement and one control at a time so as not to overload the electric pump.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – COCKPIT/ENGINE PRE-START CHECKS / Flight Controls (p.2-13–2-14)

items.question: During the AW139 FIRE WARNING TEST, pressing the BAG test pushbutton should result in which indications?
options: Only a BAG FIRE CAS warning.
MWL illumination, 'BAG FIRE' CAS warning, 'BAG' on FIRE EXTING panel, plus audio tone and 'WARNING WARNING' voice message.
Only illumination of the FIRE EXTING panel.
Only a caution message without audio.
items.explanation: The checklist describes these combined visual and aural indications when BAG is pressed during the fire warning test.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – FIRE WARNING TEST (p.2-14–2-15)

items.question: What is the purpose of the AWG TEST pushbutton in the AW139 Normal Procedures?
options: To test only the fire detection loops.
To verify the aural warning system by generating the standard set of tones and voice messages.
To test hydraulic pump pressure.
To reset CAS messages after start.
items.explanation: Pressing AWG TEST initiates the aural system test, during which various standard tones and voice messages are heard.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – AWG TEST (p.2-16)

items.question: According to AW139 ENGINE STARTING cautions, when should an engine battery start not be attempted?
options: If MAIN BUS 1 voltage is below 23 V.
If OAT is above +20 °C.
If fuel tanks are more than half full.
If rotor brake is released.
items.explanation: A caution in the ENGINE STARTING section states that a battery start should not be attempted if MAIN BUS 1 voltage is below 23 V.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – ENGINE STARTING (p.2-18A)

items.question: Which of the following is listed as a reason to ABORT an engine start in the AW139 Normal Procedures?
options: Main rotor begins to rotate before NG reaches 10 %.
Light-up does not occur within 10 seconds of selecting ENG MODE to IDLE.
ITT remains below normal start values.
Starter disengages at 35 % NG.
items.explanation: The aborted engine start procedures list several conditions, including no light-up within 10 seconds after ENG MODE is moved to IDLE.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – ABORTED ENGINE START PROCEDURES (p.2-18A)

items.question: What is the purpose of the DRY MOTORING PROCEDURE after an aborted start in the AW139?
options: To cool the main gearbox oil.
To clear internally trapped fuel and vapour before a subsequent start.
To test the rotor brake function.
To charge the main batteries.
items.explanation: Section 2 explains that the dry motoring procedure is used to clear internally trapped fuel and vapour after an aborted start.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – DRY MOTORING PROCEDURE (p.2-19)

items.question: During NORMAL ENGINE START in the AW139, which mode is recommended for normal starts?
options: MANUAL mode only.
AUTO mode is recommended for normal engine starts.
ECL OFF with manual fuel scheduling.
Any mode, as mode selection is not mentioned.
items.explanation: The NORMAL ENGINE START paragraph states that normal starts should be made using the AUTO mode; MANUAL mode has a separate procedure.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – NORMAL ENGINE START (p.2-19–2-20)

items.question: According to AW139 TAXIING procedures, what is recommended immediately after starting to taxi to verify braking action?
options: Accelerate to at least 30 kt and apply maximum braking.
Check wheel brakes at low speed and confirm symmetrical braking response.
Apply the parking brake fully and check that the helicopter stops within one rotor diameter.
Perform a full emergency stop using both wheel brakes and rotor brake simultaneously.
items.explanation: Section 2 TAXIING directs the crew to check wheel brakes shortly after taxi starts, at low speed, to verify normal and symmetrical braking.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – TAXIING

items.question: When taxiing the AW139 with nose wheel steering available, which control combination is recommended for normal turns?
options: Large rapid pedal inputs only, without cyclic.
Small pedal inputs combined with coordinated cyclic and collective as required.
Full aft cyclic and neutral pedals to pivot on the main wheels.
Collective only; pedals and cyclic are not used during taxi.
items.explanation: The TAXIING paragraph emphasises using small pedal inputs coordinated with cyclic and collective to make smooth turns without over-controlling.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – TAXIING

items.question: During AW139 TAXIING on uneven or soft surfaces, what is the recommended technique to minimise structural loads?
options: Taxi at the maximum ground speed limitation to pass the rough area quickly.
Use minimum practical taxi speed and avoid heavy braking or abrupt steering inputs.
Use maximum collective to keep most of the weight off the landing gear.
Taxi only with the nose wheel locked and brakes fully applied.
items.explanation: Normal procedures advise using minimum practical speed and avoiding heavy braking or abrupt steering on uneven or soft surfaces to limit landing gear and structural loads.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – TAXIING

items.question: In the PRE TAKE-OFF CHECKS for the AW139, how is the PARK BRK (parking brake) normally configured before take-off?
options: Set to ON throughout take-off.
Set to OFF with normal pressure check before take-off.
Left in any position; brake position is not part of the checklist.
Cycled ON/OFF three times to warm up the brakes.
items.explanation: The PRE TAKE-OFF CHECKS include confirming the parking brake OFF with a normal pressure/brake check before commencing take-off.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – PRE TAKE-OFF CHECKS

items.question: According to AW139 PRE TAKE-OFF CHECKS, what is the required configuration of the ENGINE CONTROL LEVERS (ECL) before a normal take-off?
options: Both ECLs at IDLE detent.
ENG 1 at FLIGHT and ENG 2 at IDLE.
Both ECLs at FLIGHT detent with ENG MODE switches in FLIGHT.
Both ECLs fully aft in SHUT OFF position.
items.explanation: Before a normal take-off the checklist requires both engines set to FLIGHT (ECL in FLIGHT detent, ENG MODE in FLIGHT) to ensure take-off power is available.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – PRE TAKE-OFF CHECKS / Before take-off

items.question: During a CAT B TAKE-OFF in the AW139, what is the primary objective of the initial climb segment according to Normal Procedures?
options: Maintain a low hover until reaching VNE.
Accelerate to safe OEI speed while maintaining a positive rate of climb.
Stay in ground effect and accelerate to VMINI only.
Climb vertically to 500 ft AGL before any acceleration.
items.explanation: The CAT B take-off profile aims at establishing a positive rate of climb and accelerating to a safe OEI speed in case of engine failure.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – CATEGORY B TAKE-OFF

items.question: According to AFTER TAKE-OFF / CLIMB checks, what should be verified regarding LANDING GEAR after a normal AW139 take-off?
options: Gear lever UP and three green lights still illuminated.
Gear lever UP and landing gear indications normal for retracted position.
Gear lever DOWN and nose wheel steering engaged.
Gear lever NEUTRAL and gear doors open for cooling.
items.explanation: After take-off the checklist calls for gear retraction and verifying normal indications for gear UP before continuing the climb.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – AFTER TAKE-OFF / CLIMB

items.question: In the AW139 CRUISE CHECKS, which of the following is one of the recommended pilot actions?
options: Select both generators OFF to reduce fuel consumption.
Verify engine and transmission indications within normal range and adjust power for planned cruise speed.
Set rotor speed to minimum permitted NR to reduce noise, regardless of torque.
Switch AFCS OFF for manual handling during all cruise segments.
items.explanation: The CRUISE CHECKS call for monitoring engine and transmission parameters and adjusting power to maintain the planned cruise speed within limits.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – CRUISE CHECKS

items.question: During PRE-LANDING CHECKS in the AW139, which statement best describes the checklist item for landing gear?
options: Landing gear lever DOWN with three green lights, checked before final approach.
Landing gear lever UP until crossing the threshold, then selected DOWN.
Landing gear lever NEUTRAL and doors open during approach.
Landing gear lever DOWN but green lights not required until after touchdown.
items.explanation: The PRE-LANDING CHECKS require confirmation that the gear lever is DOWN and three green lights are shown prior to final approach.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – PRE-LANDING CHECKS

items.question: According to APPROACH AND LANDING procedures, what is the recommended use of wheel brakes during the landing roll on paved surfaces?
options: Apply maximum braking immediately at touchdown regardless of speed.
Apply wheel brakes as necessary after touchdown while keeping within wheel brake limitations.
Avoid using wheel brakes; rotor drag alone must stop the helicopter.
Use parking brake ON instead of normal wheel brakes.
items.explanation: Normal procedures specify using wheel brakes as necessary during the landing roll while respecting the published wheel brake limitations.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – APPROACH AND LANDING

items.question: In POST LANDING CHECKS for the AW139, what is normally done with the AFCS (autopilot)?
options: AFCS left fully engaged until rotor stop.
AFCS disengaged and appropriate switches set to OFF as part of the post landing flow.
AFCS left in ATT mode only.
AFCS left in GA/TU mode for go-around readiness.
items.explanation: The POST LANDING CHECKS include disengaging the AFCS and setting associated switches OFF before shutdown.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – POST LANDING CHECKS

items.question: During PRE-SHUTDOWN CHECKS, what is the typical sequence for engine power levers in the AW139?
options: Both engine control levers to SHUT OFF simultaneously from FLIGHT.
One engine to IDLE, then the other to SHUT OFF immediately.
Reduce both engines to IDLE, stabilise temperatures, then move each to SHUT OFF in turn as per checklist.
Leave both engines at FLIGHT until rotor has stopped, then move to SHUT OFF.
items.explanation: Normal procedures reduce both engines to IDLE to stabilise temperatures before selecting each control lever to SHUT OFF in the prescribed order.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – PRE-SHUTDOWN CHECKS / ENGINES AND ROTOR SHUTDOWN

items.question: According to ENGINES AND ROTOR SHUTDOWN procedures, how is rotor brake use described in the basic AW139 RFM?
options: Rotor brake must always be applied immediately at engine shutdown.
Rotor brake use is optional and may be applied within the limitations stated in Section 1.
Rotor brake use is prohibited for all shutdowns.
Rotor brake may be applied only during flight idle on final approach.
items.explanation: Shutdown procedures allow rotor brake use provided it is done within the rotor brake limitations specified in Section 1.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – ENGINES AND ROTOR SHUTDOWN

items.question: In POST SHUTDOWN CHECKS, what must be verified regarding electrical power before leaving the AW139 unattended?
options: At least one generator left ON to power the CAS.
Both generators OFF but main battery ON.
All electrical power sources, including batteries, selected OFF unless required by specific procedures.
Only external power disconnected; internal power must remain ON.
items.explanation: Post shutdown checks require all electrical power sources, including batteries, to be selected OFF before the helicopter is left unattended, unless a specific procedure requires power ON.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – POST SHUTDOWN CHECKS

items.question: When performing SLOPING GROUND OPERATION – LANDING in the AW139, what is the recommended use of cyclic as the helicopter settles on an upslope?
options: Cyclic neutral at all times, regardless of slope.
Move cyclic toward the upslope to keep the rotor disc approximately perpendicular to the mast and prevent downslope skid lifting.
Move cyclic fully downslope to oppose the slope.
Apply full aft cyclic as soon as the first wheel touches.
items.explanation: The sloping ground landing technique calls for moving cyclic slightly upslope to keep the disc appropriately oriented and prevent the downslope wheel from lifting prematurely.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – SLOPING GROUND OPERATION

items.question: During SLOPING GROUND TAKE-OFF in the AW139, why does the RFM caution against rapid collective increase from a one-wheel-on-ground condition?
options: It may cause NR to increase above limits.
It may induce tail rotor stall at low airspeed.
It may lead to dynamic roll-over about the downslope wheel if lift is applied too quickly.
It may overheat the wheel brakes.
items.explanation: Slope take-off technique warns that rapid collective increase when only one wheel is on the ground can produce dynamic roll-over about that wheel.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – SLOPING GROUND OPERATION

items.question: What is the recommended technique to lift off from an upslope in the AW139 according to SLOPING GROUND TAKE-OFF procedures?
options: Raise collective rapidly while moving cyclic downslope to pivot off the uphill wheel.
Increase collective slowly while moving cyclic toward level attitude, allowing the downslope wheel to leave the ground first.
Apply full aft cyclic before raising collective.
Raise collective with cyclic fixed in neutral to minimise control inputs.
items.explanation: The RFM describes increasing collective slowly while moving cyclic to maintain a level attitude, so the downslope wheel leaves the ground first and dynamic roll-over is avoided.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – SLOPING GROUND OPERATION

items.question: In the AW139 Normal Procedures, what is the general recommendation regarding use of AFCS during instrument approaches?
options: AFCS must always be OFF during all instrument approaches.
AFCS may be used in accordance with AFCS and approach procedure limitations to reduce pilot workload.
AFCS may only be used for go-arounds, not for approaches.
AFCS use is limited to cruise and is prohibited below 500 ft AGL.
items.explanation: Normal procedures allow AFCS use on instrument approaches provided the operation complies with AFCS limitations and procedure requirements, helping to reduce pilot workload.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – APPROACH AND LANDING / instrument approaches

items.question: During the DAILY FUEL DRAIN CHECK, what additional precaution is mentioned in the AW139 RFM when contamination is suspected?
options: Increase the drained quantity well above 20 cc from each sump until fuel runs clear.
Skip the drain check and rely on fuel filters only.
Perform the check only after taxi to stir the fuel in the tanks.
Use only visual inspection through the filler caps without draining.
items.explanation: The description notes that if contamination is suspected, a larger quantity than the nominal 10–20 cc may need to be drained until fuel is free of contamination.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – DAILY FUEL DRAIN CHECK

items.question: When planning AW139 flights in cold weather, what is one of the NORMAL PROCEDURES recommendations before starting engines after prolonged exposure to very low temperatures?
options: Carry out an engine start with no preheat to test engine capability.
Ensure that oil and hydraulic fluids have been brought within acceptable temperature limits by appropriate preheat or hangar storage.
Only check that fuel tanks are at least half full; fluid temperature is not relevant.
Plan to operate only one engine to reduce thermal shock.
items.explanation: Cold weather procedures recommend ensuring that engine oil and other fluids are within acceptable temperature limits, using hangar storage or preheat as required, before starting the engines.
references: AW139 RFM Sec 2 – COLD WEATHER OPERATION
